positions.position: Assenting to the truth of God's promise also entails seeking it and acting accordingly.
positions.reasons: Al-Biqāʿī defines taṣdīq as assent that makes the informant's statement true for the believer. Qatāda says one believes God's promise and works for it. Elmalılı requires practical, sincere pursuit of goodness; Ibn ʿĀshūr says acknowledgment implies desire to attain the promise and deeds leading to success, in contrast to denial in 92:9. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says truthfulness can concern words, deeds, intention and belief; Qur'anic affirmation commonly concerns God, His signs, messengers, words and meeting.

question: What is the form and lexical sense of al-ḥusnā?

positions.position: It is the feminine superlative of aḥsan, literally 'the best' or 'most beautiful,' with an understood feminine noun.
positions.reasons: Jishumī calls it the supreme blessing for its excellent outcome. Ibn ʿĀshūr allows an omitted noun such as reward, victory, promise or outcome; Islāḥī supplies ʿāqibah, fate or outcome. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ distinguishes material beauty from moral good and cites al-Rāghib's distinction: ḥusn applies to objects and events, ḥasana as a noun to events, and ḥusnā only to events; she notes its opposition to sawʾa.

question: What does al-ḥusnā refer to in this verse?

positions.position: God's promised replacement or compensation for what the giver spends.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṭabarī prefers this because the preceding giver seeks recompense and the angel report prays for replacement; al-Qurṭubī reports this preference. Al-Rāzī cites 34:39 and 2:261: replacement exceeds spending, while doubting it is bad opinion of God. Abū Ḥayyān specifies a sworn promise of reward in this world; al-Ālūsī reports worldly return with increase. Ibn ʿAṭiyya points to the angels' prayer.

positions.position: The testimony of God's oneness, 'there is no god but God.'
positions.reasons: Al-Rāzī says giving and restraint do not avail without faith in unity and prophecy, citing 90:14–17. Al-Bayḍāwī calls this a true, beautiful statement. Al-Biqāʿī extends the word of justice to monotheism's implications: afterlife promises, replacement in this life, Islam's eventual dominance and the Messenger's promises. Al-Ālūsī prefers tawḥīd together with all required beliefs in a comprehensive account of giving, piety and faith. Study Quran attributes the testimony to most commentators.

positions.position: Paradise, the finest reward.
positions.reasons: Mujāhid and others cite 10:26, which promises al-ḥusnā and more to good doers; Study Quran cites 3:148 and 3:195. Ubayy b. Kaʿb reports the Prophet directly answering 'Paradise' when asked, with Ibn Kathīr giving no grading. Al-Rāzī treats reward and Paradise as equivalent here.

positions.position: Reward or recompense in general.
positions.reasons: Al-Qurṭubī says the proposed meanings converge on reward, ultimately Paradise; al-Rāzī likewise equates reward with Paradise. Qatāda relates recompense to the giving and piety just mentioned; Khuṣayf gives the general gloss.

positions.position: God's promise to reward the believer, without specifying the reward.
positions.reasons: Qatāda says the believer trusts God's promise and acts for it; al-Baghawī notes that God will fulfill it. Al-Bayḍāwī calls it the true, good promise.

positions.position: The beautiful religion of Islam.
positions.reasons: Al-Ālūsī reports this from ʿIkrima and a group, also from Ibn ʿAbbās.

positions.position: Faith or the creed as a whole.
positions.reasons: Sayyid Quṭb calls al-ḥusnā an identifying designation of the creed. Kur'an Yolu prefers the whole of Islamic belief and practice, including creed, worship, social dealings and ethics. Study Quran notes a gloss of belief in God. Al-Ālūsī includes all required beliefs in his preferred comprehensive reading.

positions.position: Prayer, almsgiving and fasting.
positions.reasons: This gloss is attributed to Zayd b. Aslam; Ibn Kathīr separately transmits from him the end-of-Ramadan charity.

positions.position: The blessings God has bestowed on the person.
positions.reasons: Māwardī and Ibn al-Jawzī attribute this to ʿAṭāʾ; Ibn Kathīr reports it from ʿIkrima.

positions.position: The best or good outcome promised for virtuous deeds.
positions.reasons: Elmalılı prefers the better reward and final outcome, or the verses promising it, citing 10:26 and 29:7; he also cites 42:23, 53:31, 12:56 and 2:58 for enlarged recompense. Islāḥī supplies the omitted noun 'outcome': spending and goodness bring good results. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says this wide sense encompasses monotheism, Paradise and both worldly and otherworldly recompense.

positions.position: Every good quality or real moral good.
positions.reasons: Al-Qaffāl cites 9:52, 42:23 and 41:50 for good outcomes and increased reward. Elmalılı says the believer distinguishes virtue from vice. Asad calls ultimate good an absolute moral imperative independent of time and society.

positions.position: The goodness and beneficial purposes of God's prescribed bodily and financial worship.
positions.reasons: Al-Rāzī joins giving for God and avoiding prohibitions to affirming the laws' beneficial ends.

positions.position: A beautiful true statement, including the Qur'an or any word conveying truth.
positions.reasons: Al-Biqāʿī calls it the excellent word of justice and includes monotheism and all divine promises. Al-Ālūsī reports any truth-bearing word; Elmalılı gives the Qur'an as an example.

positions.position: The obligatory charity at the end of Ramadan.
positions.reasons: A distinct report from Zayd b. Aslam gives this narrower duty.

positions.position: Prayer specifically.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿĀshūr reports it as one of the particular identifications.

positions.position: Almsgiving specifically.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿĀshūr reports it as one of the particular identifications.

positions.position: The oath affirmed in the passage.
positions.reasons: Al-Naḥḥās reports this from Ibn ʿAbbās, calls its chain reliable and regards it as suited to context.

positions.position: The final world.
Forgiveness of grave sinners.
The Prophet's intercession.
Sincerity.
Gnosis.
positions.reasons: Al-Sulamī attributes this inward gloss to Sahl.

positions.position: Well-being here and forgiveness in the next life.
The highest rank of spiritual perfection.
positions.reasons: Qāshānī says certain intellectual faith in perfection makes spiritual ascent possible.

positions.position: God Himself.
positions.reasons: Study Quran connects this to God's Most Beautiful Names in 17:110, 20:8, 59:24 and 7:180.

turns_on: Whether the feminine superlative designates a creed or truthful word, a promised result, a particular act, divine gifts, or a broad good; some sources explicitly treat several glosses as convergent.

question: Why are giving and piety mentioned before affirmation?

positions.position: Affirmation follows piety as a specific instance of a general virtue; its position also preserves the verse ending.
positions.reasons: Al-Ālūsī acknowledges faith's importance while explaining its later placement by the general-to-specific order and rhyme.

positions.position: Giving and piety come first because practical deeds establish the affirmation and lead to its promised result.
positions.reasons: Elmalılı says belief precedes deeds in the order of being; the text puts deeds first because verbal belief without them does not earn ease and because effects and recompense follow their causes.

positions.position: Giving heads the paired clauses because it is foundational for the faith and piety or denial and self-sufficiency that follow.
positions.reasons: Al-Irshād notes that giving ranks lower than the later traits yet founds their paired descriptions.

positions.position: Giving obedience and avoiding idolatry could be understood as acts that precede faith.
positions.reasons: Al-Ālūsī rejects this explanation: 'giving' conventionally concerns money, especially when opposed to withholding, and the proposed sequence remains unexplained. He also rejects counting listening to learn monotheism as giving and avoidance of shirk as piety.

turns_on: How the order relates to belief's logical priority, the practical acts, the verse ending and the paired opposite clause.

question: What does this affirmation teach about conduct and its result?

positions.position: Faith in God's good reward motivates giving, piety and perseverance toward the Hereafter.
positions.reasons: Al-Rāzī says the paired paths lead to praiseworthy or blameworthy outcomes. Elmalılı says expectation of a better afterlife makes sacrifice joyful, citing 59:9 and 64:16. Islāḥī says faith in reward moves one to give for God rather than worldly gain, citing 107:1–3; the struggle against desire grows strength and leads to the company and Paradise of 89:29–30.

positions.position: The three traits express the person's effort toward purification, met by God's freely willed aid.
positions.reasons: Sayyid Quṭb says success depends on God's aid despite the person's utmost effort.

positions.position: Giving covers financial worship, piety covers obedience and avoidance of sin, and affirmation covers comprehensive faith.
positions.reasons: Al-Ālūsī prefers the triad because together it covers all endeavors; al-Biqāʿī specifies giving what God commands and guarding oneself through obedience and avoidance.

question: How is this verse read inwardly?

positions.position: Abū Bakr's giving included self and wealth, refusal to settle into the natural self, and affirmation of monotheism.
positions.reasons: Tustarī reports this from Abū Bakr.

positions.position: The generous renounce attachment to both abodes, avoid frivolity and doubt, and seek nearness to God.
Certain faith in the rank of perfection makes ascent possible, and God eases the seeker by cutting attachments and strengthening certainty.
positions.reasons: Qāshānī joins intellectual certainty to God's assistance on the easy path.

question: Who or what occasion is reported for this passage?

positions.position: Abū Bakr freed vulnerable converts despite his father's advice to free strong protectors, seeking God's reward or face.
positions.reasons: Al-Farrāʾ gives nine enslaved men bought from polytheists; other reports emphasize weak women or elderly converts. Abū Quḥāfa wanted strong allies, but Abū Bakr sought divine reward or God's face. Al-Ālūsī says al-Ḥākim authenticated the version he cites. Ibn Isḥāq and family reports vary in the father's wording; one report extends the revelation to 'he will be satisfied'.

positions.position: Abū Bakr bought and freed Bilāl from Umayya, and their opposed efforts are contrasted.
positions.reasons: Al-Baghawī's anonymous report says the price was a garment and ten coins; Ibn Masʿūd's account also names Ubayy among the opponents. The good is identified as monotheism and the hard outcome as Hell; the contrast relates to 92:4.

positions.position: Abū Bakr is the giver and Abū Sufyān the denier in a report about spending and resurrection.
positions.reasons: In Muqātil's report Abū Bakr hopes for forgiveness and promises to remind Abū Sufyān at Saqar; Abū Sufyān mocks resurrection and says spent wealth is lost. The Durr report through al-Kalbī and Abū Ṣāliḥ names them as contrasting figures.

positions.position: Abū al-Daḥdāḥ traded his garden for a palm whose owner had refused the Prophet's offer of a tree in Paradise, then gave it to the poor neighbor.
positions.reasons: ʿAṭāʾ reports the fruit fell into a neighbor's home and the owner refused the Prophet's offer. The giver is Abū al-Daḥdāḥ and the miser the Anṣārī owner; their ease and hardship lead to Paradise and Hell, while death removes the miser's wealth. Al-Ālūsī notes a similar occasion.

positions.position: An unnamed believer traded forty palms for a stingy owner's tree and gave it to a poor family.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿAbbās's report gives forty palms as the price and a promised palm in Paradise for the buyer.

positions.position: The passage was revealed in connection with the angels' prayer for the spender and against the miser.
positions.reasons: Reports differ on sunset versus sunrise; the shared prayer requests compensation for the spender and ruin for the withholder. Al-Māwardī states no grading.

turns_on: Different reported persons, transactions and prayers are connected to the revelation.

question: What does the angel report say about spenders and misers?

positions.position: At sunset two angels pray for the spender's replacement and the miser's loss.
positions.reasons: Abū al-Dardāʾ transmits this from the Prophet. Al-Thaʿlabī and al-Rāzī say the call reaches all creation except humans and jinn; Ibn ʿAṭiyya states no grading.

positions.position: At sunrise or each morning two angels pray for replacement and ruin.
positions.reasons: Al-Māwardī transmits a sunrise version through Qatāda, Khulayd and Abū al-Dardāʾ without grading; al-Qurṭubī reports a morning version from Abū Hurayra.

turns_on: The reports differ on sunset versus sunrise or morning.

question: Does a reported occasion confine the verse to its named people?

positions.position: The passage's teaching is general despite specific occasion reports.
positions.reasons: Al-Rāzī cites the general claim that human striving differs and the warning of blazing fire in 92:4 and 92:14. Kur'an Yolu says the message and rulings remain general.

question: How do the cited verses bear on written destiny and action?

positions.position: Destinations and deeds are decreed, yet people must act; each is facilitated toward the work and path for which they were created.
positions.reasons: ʿAlī's funeral report says each place in Paradise or Hell is recorded; the Prophet rejects reliance on that record and recites 92:5–10. Versions from al-Nazzāl, Saʿd b. ʿUbayda, Jābir and Bashīr say every worker is made ready for decreed work; a man asks after 54:49 whether acts are new or fixed. Suraqa asks the same in Jābir's version. Shuʿba notes Manṣūr's corroborating transmission through Sulaymān al-Aʿmash.

question: How does the passage connect to its surrounding verses and sūra?

positions.position: Its opposed lists pair giving with stinginess, piety with self-sufficiency, affirmation with denial, and ease with hardship.
positions.reasons: Corpus Coranicum notes the symmetrical behavior-to-consequence sequences, cross-rhyme from vowel variation and first-person divine promise authorized beside the oath; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says the oath's night, daylight and creation frame opposed earthly efforts and afterlife fates.

positions.position: The final stanza reverses the earlier saved-and-damned order while echoing its conduct and outcomes.
positions.reasons: Corpus Coranicum points to ittaqā in 92:5 and atqā in 92:17; the first pair lists conduct before outcomes, while the final pair puts warning and promise before conduct.

positions.position: The sūra spells out traits of success and failure announced in the preceding sūra.
positions.reasons: Abū Ḥayyān relates it to 91:9–10, then to the Fire and those spared it.

positions.position: The contrasting paths exemplify divine preparation for obedience and disbelief.
positions.reasons: Al-Zamakhsharī compares easing toward obedience to saddling and bridling a horse and cites 6:125 on opening the heart to Islam.

positions.position: The Prophet cites these verses among scriptural descriptions of Paradise.
positions.reasons: The cited report also invokes 32:17 for unseen delights and 56:30 for the tree's shade.

question: How is the preceding relative pronoun parsed?

positions.position: Basran grammarians take man as the subject.
positions.reasons: Al-Naḥḥās records this analysis.

positions.position: Kufan grammarians take the resumptive pronoun attached to the following verb as its syntactic support.
positions.reasons: Al-Naḥḥās records this alternative.

turns_on: Basran and Kufan parsing of man and its resumptive pronoun.
